h: From the vote to the street: women now want space on their own terms
dek: According to Sohini Sengupta, the movement that began with the demand for Gyanesh Kumar's resignation has become a fight for women's right to public spaces.
body: In her article in Navjivan, Sohini Sengupta writes that the October movement began with a demand for electoral accountability. The demand was that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar take responsibility for the irregularities in SIR and resign. According to the writer, about 13 crore voters' names were removed from the rolls in it. But within a few days this fight spread to another question: can women be on the street on their own terms or not.

The writer lists the events. On 3 October in Delhi, three women journalists complained of sexual harassment. Over the weekend of 10-11 October, police detained thousands of people, citing orders under Section 163 of the BNSS, and surrounded Jantar Mantar. A woman journalist accused ACP Vivek Bhagat of misconduct. The very next day came the order for his promotion, which was later put on hold pending an inquiry. Several women, including AISA president Neha Bora, also spoke of similar treatment.

According to the article, at Connaught Place right-wing men harassed protesting women and drove them away, and then walked off without anyone stopping them. It was only some women wearing the hijab who were stopped on the way and had their phones taken.

Sengupta also draws attention to the law. Section 43(5) of the BNSS generally bars the arrest of a woman after sunset and before sunrise, except in special circumstances and with the prior approval of a magistrate. In her view, police reaching a girl sitting at home at eleven at night is no such special circumstance.

The article concludes that the new generation of women is fearless in its slogans, refuses to become any party's poster girl, and is challenging power, the police, politicians' rhetoric and online hate, all at once.
nazar: This article reminds us that the right to vote and the right to walk the street without fear are not separate. In a system where asking about names cut from the voter list becomes a crime, a woman simply sitting at home at night also becomes unsafe.
The most important point is that these women do not want to become any party's shield. The opposition has to learn from this movement, not take it over.
sawal: Who will protect the women who came out to save the vote?
ref: BNSS Section 163
A provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita that lets the administration ban gatherings in an area. It replaced Section 144 of the old CrPC.
BNSS Section 43(5)
A rule on the arrest of women: arrest after sunset and before sunrise only in special circumstances, with the prior approval of a magistrate.
ank: Names removed in SIR, according to the writer

h: 13 crore names cut, but free ration still goes to 80 crore
dek: Mahendra Pandey asks how, if so many people have died or gone missing, the government's other counts have stayed exactly the same.
body: In this sharp article in Navjivan, Mahendra Pandey begins with a social analyst's remark that the Indian people are comfortable with slavery. According to the writer, today's situation seems to prove this true, and this mental slavery has spread not just among the people but to the judiciary, the executive, the legislature and the media.

The writer alleges that after losing its majority in 2024, the BJP fears losing the next election, so it needed a trusted officer for the revision of the voter rolls, and this is how Gyanesh Kumar rose. In his view the Election Commission stands fully with the government: the opposition's complaints go unheard, and no action is taken on hate speeches by BJP leaders.

The most solid part of the article is about the figures. The opposition questioned the removal of 13.39 crore names in three phases. In reply the commission said 2.80 crore were dead, 3.01 crore were not found at their address, 6.30 crore had moved elsewhere for good and 1.02 crore had two or more voter cards. The writer says that about 22 percent of people being untraceable shows the government does not even know where its own citizens are.

Then he catches a contradiction. Since 2021 the prime minister has kept saying that 80 crore people get free grain, and by 2026 this number had not changed. If voters are dying, moving away or disappearing, how has the count of beneficiaries stayed exactly the same? And despite the claim that 25 crore people have come out of poverty, free ration continues.
The writer concludes that the Election Commission is now the ruling party's only remaining support, and hopes that voters will break the chains of slavery.
nazar: In many places the article's anger runs ahead of the figures, but its core question is fair. The four parts the commission gave add up to about 13.13 crore, which means about 26 lakh names in the 13.39 crore figure need to be accounted for separately.
Two counts from the same government, one with crores of names missing and another with 80 crore beneficiaries holding steady, cannot both stand. Accountability should begin with this contradiction.
sawal: If voters went down, why didn't ration receivers go down?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision: the Election Commission's intensive revision of the voter list, in which details and documents are collected afresh from every voter.
Free grain scheme
The Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana, under which the central government claims to give free ration to about 80 crore people.

h: 10 October: the day Delhi was turned into a prison
dek: T Naveen argues that if the 10 October march really was a failure, why did it take thousands of security personnel, shut metro stations and thousands of arrests to stop it.
body: Independent writer T Naveen writes in Countercurrents that the real meaning of 10 October lies not in counting the crowd at Jantar Mantar but in the arrangements made to stop people from getting there. There were three demands: the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, a halt to SIR, and the protection of democracy.

According to the writer, news reports said metro stations in Delhi were shut, rail routes were disrupted and about 43,000 personnel of the BSF, CRPF and Delhi Police were deployed. It is alleged that resident welfare associations were told to stop people, and mosques and gurdwaras were told not to feed the protesters. Some reports put the number of people detained as high as seven thousand, which the writer himself says needs checking.

He also points to the police's double standards. Students were picked up on mere suspicion, while it is alleged that Bajrang Dal members attacked student protesters and the police did not act properly. The writer demands an independent inquiry into this and compares it to the British crackdown on the 1942 Quit India Movement: arrests can stop a movement, but they cannot wipe out its cause.

On SIR the article is balanced. Cleaning up the list is necessary, but it should be transparent and should not leave out any eligible citizen. For someone whose name is cut and who has no working way to fix it, the right to vote remains only on paper. The writer believes the demand to remove the commissioner is political and not proof of wrongdoing, but the commission should explain its process.

BJP leaders and right-wing social media called the march a flop. The writer's answer is direct: when the way to get there is itself blocked, public feeling cannot be measured by the size of the crowd. Barricades and detention vans are no answer to the questions that had drawn people to Delhi.
nazar: The government cannot say two things at once: that the protest had no strength, and that the whole capital had to be sealed off to stop it. This contradiction is itself proof of the movement's strength. What lesson in democracy is being taught to the young people called the country's future, by putting them in detention vans?
The allegations of selective policing are the most serious. If the law moves according to political colour, the claim of maintaining public order also becomes hollow.
sawal: Why 43,000 personnel to stop a failed march?
ref: Quit India Movement (1942)
A movement against British rule at Gandhi's call, in which top leaders were jailed overnight, yet the movement kept spreading.
Article 19
The part of the Constitution that gives the freedom to speak and to assemble peacefully without arms, subject only to 'reasonable restrictions'.

h: From Ekwari to Jantar Mantar: the long roots of Neha Bora's politics
dek: Through a story running from Bhojpur's Naxalbari era to AISA, a Caravan India analysis asks why strength on the street does not turn into votes.
body: This Caravan India analysis looks at the rise of AISA president Neha Bora by linking it to the history of the CPI (ML) Liberation. On 4 October, during a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, Delhi Police took the 29-year-old research student away from Jantar Mantar, while women climbed onto the vehicle to try to stop it. The article asks where this public support comes from and why it does not turn into votes.

The story begins in Ekwari village in Bhojpur, where Dalit, backward-caste and landless labourers rose against upper-caste landlords under the leadership of Master Jagdish Mahto and Rameshwar Ahir. According to the article, in 1967 Mahto was beaten while trying to stop election rigging, and this is what pushed him onto the Naxal path. The issues were dignity, wages paid in khesari (a cheap lentil), and the exploitation of women. After this a cycle of violence ran for decades, with massacres from Danwar-Bihta to Bathani Tola.

The village's memory is still divided. An elderly Bhumihar calls it a game of power, while a young Dalit man and an elderly woman say this very fight gave them the freedom to protest, and women began going to school and the market without fear. After 1978-79 the party turned from the underground path to open electoral politics.

The election figures show a slow climb: 11.06 percent in 2014, 38.79 percent in 2019, and in 2024, in alliance with the RJD and Congress, a win in the Arrah seat with 48.28 percent of the vote. The article sees Mandal politics as a big reason, which pulled the middle castes away from class struggle towards caste politics.
Villagers see the party as a force that brought them dignity, but often give their vote to someone else. The article's question is whether Neha Bora's appeal will be able to bridge this gap.
nazar: This article reminds us that the anger seen at Jantar Mantar did not arise suddenly. The fight at Ekwari too was sparked by a protest against election rigging, and today's fight too is about the right to vote.
The real test of the movement is whether it can carry the dignity won on the street into a share in institutions. For that it needs the language of both caste and class.
sawal: Why does the respect won on the street not reach the ballot box?
ref: CPI (ML) Liberation
A Left party that came out of the Naxalbari movement and has been in electoral politics since the 1990s. AISA is its student organisation.
Bathani Tola massacre
In 1996, according to the article, 22 Dalits were killed in an attack by the Ranvir Sena in Bathani Tola in Bhojpur.

h: Seen from across the border: 13 crore names missing, Jantar Mantar locked
dek: Pakistani writer Manoj Kumar Lohana argues that when crores of names are cut from the voter list and even the set place for protest is shut, the question is no longer about one officer but about the structure of democracy.
body: In the Lahore magazine The Friday Times, Manoj Kumar Lohana opens his piece on India's movement with a small incident. Delhi Police caught some other woman, taking her for AISA president Neha Bora, while the real Neha had crossed the barricades and reached Vijay Chowk. For the writer, this is a picture of a state so absorbed in fixing identities that it picks up the wrong person.

Then he turns to the figures. According to the commission's own data, about 13.3 crore names were cut from the draft lists. Of these, about 2.8 crore were said to be dead and one crore duplicates, but close to nine and a half crore went into the 'absent', 'permanently shifted' or 'other' columns. In Hyderabad's Malakpet seat, it was reported that more names were cut than the number of votes cast in 2023. At one booth in Chandni Chowk, 908 out of 909 voters were removed. A study in Nandigram found that 95 percent of the names cut were Muslim.

The writer accepts that some of the BJP's arguments have weight: crores of names may really be of dead people or duplicates, the Supreme Court approved SIR in May, and the old allegations about EVMs were not proved. But in his view this does not settle why crores of people were treated as 'absent', why two election commissioners reportedly recorded objections about 14 times in ten months, and why protesters were kept away from their set place.

His stress is on the flaw in the structure. The 2023 law removed the Chief Justice from the selection committee and gave the government a two-to-one majority, and Gyanesh Kumar is the first Chief Election Commissioner appointed under this law. If one team chooses the referee, every decision is bound to be doubted. He calls Jantar Mantar a compromise: power will put up with criticism in one place. Sealing it off completely is going back on that compromise.

In the end the writer reminds us that the BJP itself grew out of the JP movement, the Rath Yatra and Anna Hazare's sit-ins. Protest is not a fault of democracy, it is its feedback. Gyanesh Kumar's resignation too will not bring back a single cut name; the real question is the method of appointment, and a process that puts the burden of proving eligibility on a voter who is already registered.
nazar: This article written from across the border stings because it gives room to the BJP's arguments too, and still reaches the same conclusion as the people on the street. The voter list decides who is counted in the country. When this count goes most heavily against the poor, migrant workers and Muslims, it is not a clean-up, it is a weeding out.

It will not be enough for the movement's demand to stay stuck on Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. Restoring balance to the selection committee and making public every reason for cutting a name: that is the real fight.
sawal: If one team chooses the referee, how can anyone trust the game?
ref: SIR (Special Intensive Revision)
The Election Commission's fresh check of the voter list, which began in Bihar in July 2025 and spread across the country. Voters were asked for documents in it.
The 2023 Election Commissioners law
This law put a Union minister in place of the Chief Justice on the committee that selects commissioners, creating a majority in the prime minister's favour.

h: Memes, songs and satyagraha: Gen Z has shown the way
dek: Human rights activist Father Cedric Prakash says this generation, which joins laughter and songs with Gandhi's methods, has begun to frighten those in power.
body: Father Cedric Prakash, a well-known human rights activist from Gujarat, reads this movement in Countercurrents as the awakening of a generation. He starts in May 2026, when a remark by Chief Justice Surya Kant brought the word 'cockroach' into debate and Abhijeet Dipke formed the Cockroach Janta Party as satire. This account, which began with memes, became a movement of lakhs of people. It first forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and has now taken aim at the Chief Election Commissioner.

According to the writer, this year Gandhi Jayanti did not remain an official ritual. On 2 October in Ahmedabad, the home ground of the prime minister and the home minister, more than two hundred young people gathered at the gate of Gujarat University and demanded the removal of the Chief Election Commissioner. Some were detained. In these young people singing, dancing and reading poetry, the writer hears an echo of 1942's 'Do or Die'.

He mentions the press conference at the Delhi Press Club on 7 October, where AISA's Neha Bora, CJP's Saurav Das, and leaders of SFI and AISF sat. According to the writer, they left professional spokespersons behind, and he quips that the prime minister has not held a single open press conference to this day. When asked about money, one protester sarcastically named the PM CARES Fund, and the questioner himself ended up on the defensive.

The article also records the incident of 13 October, when Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and Ajinkya Shinde entered the cordoned-off Jantar Mantar carrying the tricolour and were detained. Police had already removed Jantar Mantar from the list of protest sites and suggested Ramlila Maidan, Burari and the CBD Ground. On 10 October, when the roads were closed, Neha Bora turned people towards Dilli Haat and sent a message from detention that she was locked up, not the movement.

The writer accepts that countless movements, including farmers', are going on in the country, but what sets this generation apart is its internet-born style: memes, dark humour, answering rumours on Instagram. In his eyes this generation is fighting for the values of the Constitution against corruption, communalism, exclusion and electoral wrongdoing, and the government is afraid of it.
nazar: The movement that power took for a joke has made power uneasy with its jokes. Answering satire with barricades and Tihar shows that humour is still the sharpest political weapon. The credit for taking Gandhi out of ritual and onto the street also goes to this generation.
But the article's enthusiasm leaves a question: will the energy born of memes last into the dull, ground-level fight over the voter list, where cut names have to be added back booth by booth?
sawal: Will the energy of memes reach the fight at the booth?
ref: Cockroach Janta Party
A satirical social media platform formed in May 2026 in response to a remark by the Chief Justice, which turned into a youth movement. Its founder is Abhijeet Dipke.
PM CARES Fund
A relief fund in the prime minister's name set up during Covid. Questions have kept being raised over its accounts being outside RTI and audit.

h: A spelling mistake, and out of the vote: the real story of SIR
dek: An Internet Freedom Foundation analysis shows that a third of Delhi's voters were left out of the draft list, and in Bengal names were added back in 91 percent of the appeals that got a decision.
body: In the last part of its three-part series on SIR, the Internet Freedom Foundation, a group working on digital rights, has asked whose names were cut, whether they were cut correctly, and why a voter cannot check the list for themselves. According to the group, 32.78 percent of voters in Delhi were left out of the draft list, more than in any other state. 47.56 lakh people were left out and more than 33 lakh got notices.

The sharpest part of the analysis is about who bears the burden. The software gets stuck on the spelling of names: 'Mohammad' and 'Md.' are taken to be different people, and different spellings of Adivasi (indigenous) names become a reason for a notice. Citing reports, the group says that in Delhi's Muslim-majority seats and seats reserved for Scheduled Castes, 20 to 45 percent of names were cut, and in Nandigram 95 percent of the names cut were Muslim.

The commission has kept presenting 'zero appeals' in Bihar as proof of its accuracy. The group reads it the other way round. An RTI in Bengal showed that by 7 August only two percent of more than 38 lakh appeals had been decided, and in 91 percent of those the voter's name was added back. In other words, the absence of appeals is proof not of correct pruning but of a closed door.

The state of the ground workers is recorded too. In Delhi about 14,000 BLOs are handling this work on their own phones, and a single one may have close to two hundred and fifty notices. On 26 September the commission announced reliefs such as collecting documents at home, but according to the group these offer nothing to those whose names have already been cut. They are being told to fill Form 6 like new applicants.

The last argument is about transparency. Booth-wise lists of people marked absent, dead or duplicate are public, but the full voter list is not given in a machine-readable form, citing privacy. The old 2002-03 lists are scanned images, in which two retired officers could not find their own names. The group is now using RTI to ask for the criteria used to flag names and the figures for every seat.
nazar: The anger at Jantar Mantar is not in the air; this analysis shows the solid ground under it. When a machine tells 'Md.' and 'Mohammad' apart and the result is a citizen losing the vote, it no longer remains a technical slip. The blow has fallen hardest on those who have little of both papers and time: Muslims, Dalits, Adivasis and migrant workers.
The most important demand is the simplest: the full list and the reason for every cut name should be public. Why should anyone expect to trust a commission that will not do even this much?
sawal: Why must the person whose name was cut become a new voter?
ref: BLO (Booth Level Officer)
A worker appointed for each polling station, usually a school teacher or anganwadi worker, who goes door to door to do the voter list work.
Form 6
The application form for becoming a voter for the first time. It is alleged that people already registered whose names were cut are also being asked to fill it.

h: A hundred years of Tiruchanur: the temple door opened, the doors of power did not
dek: A 1925 court case over a Dalit devotee lighting a lamp in a temple shows that the fight for equality has now shifted to courts and universities.
body: On 13 October 1925, at the Sri Padmavathi Ammavari temple in Tiruchanur near Tirupati, a Dalit devotee named Murugesan went inside and lit a camphor lamp. For this 'crime' he was arrested, held in the Tirupati sub-jail and tried under Section 295 of the Indian Penal Code. Nikhil Sanjay-Rekha Adsule, who writes on constitutional law, has written in The Wire on the centenary of this event that it was a direct challenge to the system of untouchability and ritual purity, running in the same period as the Vaikom Satyagraha.

The lower court found Murugesan guilty. The appeal was heard in Chittoor in December 1925, where C. Rajagopalachari, who had given up legal practice because of the Non-Cooperation Movement, arrived in khadi to argue for him. His argument was simple: how can a man who came to worship insult religion, and no one was harmed either. According to the writer, the magistrate set aside the sentence. The ruling was not binding on other courts, but its symbolic weight was great.

The article places Tiruchanur in a larger chain of temple entry struggles: the Ambadevi temple satyagraha in Amravati in 1927, and the Kalaram temple satyagraha in Nashik in 1930, led by Ambedkar. The writer also shows the difference between the South's path of legal persuasion and Ambedkar's demand for equal citizenship.

These movements left their mark on the Constituent Assembly. Article 17 abolished untouchability, and Article 25(2)(b) gave the state the power to open Hindu public religious institutions to all. But the writer argues that exclusion has now moved from the temple into the institutions of power. He recalls the deaths of Rohith Vemula and Darshan Solanki and puts forward figures given in the Rajya Sabha in March 2025: of 715 High Court judges appointed since 2018, only 22 were from Scheduled Castes and 16 from Scheduled Tribes. In his view the victory of 1925 is incomplete.
nazar: The story of Tiruchanur reminds us that making a law against untouchability and getting equality are two different things. Today a Dalit is not jailed for entering a temple, but from university hostels to the High Court bench the doors are still narrow.
When the government itself says there is no provision for reservation in the appointment of judges, the question is what the judiciary is doing to bring diversity within itself.
sawal: When will Dalits reach the High Court bench?
ref: Vaikom Satyagraha
A movement in 1924-25 in Vaikom, Travancore, for the right of Dalits and 'avarna' (outside the caste order) castes to walk on the roads around the temple.
Kalaram temple satyagraha
A satyagraha in March 1930 for the entry of Dalits into the Kalaram temple in Nashik, led by Ambedkar and Bhaurao Gaikwad.

h: The sale of IDBI: the public bore the losses, the profits go to private hands
dek: The decision to hand control of IDBI Bank, rescued with public money, to a foreign private group raises questions both about a promise made to Parliament and about social banking.
body: On 14 October the central government approved the sale of its and LIC's combined 60.72 percent stake in IDBI Bank to a company linked to Canada's Fairfax Financial Holdings. Devidas Tuljapurkar, convenor of the joint forum of IDBI officers and employees, has written in The Wire that this is not just a matter of selling shares but a question of public investment, accountability to Parliament and economic sovereignty.

The writer recalls that IDBI was set up in 1964 as a development finance institution, which gave long-term money to steel, cement and basic industries. When it was made a commercial bank in 2004, the then finance minister Jaswant Singh assured both Houses of Parliament that the government would in all circumstances keep at least a 51 percent stake. The writer asks what has now happened to that promise, and on the basis of what study the policy was changed.

The government's argument is that the bank repeatedly needed public capital and private capital will make it stronger. According to the writer the picture is the opposite: in 2020-21 the bank's net profit was about 1,359 crore rupees, which rose to about 9,513 crore in 2025-26. When the public sector carried the risk and the bank returned to profit, why should its future earnings go into private hands? The writer calls this nationalising losses and privatising profits.

He also reminds us that public sector banks carry more than 90 percent of the load of schemes such as Jan Dhan, Mudra, crop loans and direct cash transfers. Private ownership is no guarantee of good management, and to show this he lists recent controversies at several private banks.

The writer's demand is that the deal be stopped for now, the bank's condition, valuation and options be placed before Parliament, and binding safeguards be fixed for employees, customers, rural branches and reservation policy.
nazar: Public sector banks reach the village branch, the small farmer and the trader with no credit history, because their aim is not only profit. Handing a profit-making public bank to a foreign private group is a step back from this idea, and if it becomes a precedent, the turn of other public sector banks may come too.
A promise made in Parliament is the government's word. Breaking it without debate weakens democratic accountability.
sawal: Where did the 51 percent promise made in Parliament go?
ref: Development finance institution
A public institution that gives long-term loans to industry and infrastructure, where profits come late and risks are higher.
Bank nationalisation
In 1969 the government took over 14 private banks, and six more in 1980, so that credit would reach farming, small industry and jobs.

h: Why the fear of books near the puja pandal?
dek: Using the action and attacks on Left book stalls in Bengal during Durga Puja, Sabrang India asks whose goodwill the right to put forward ideas in a public place depends on.
body: Left book stalls near Durga Puja pandals (temporary shrines) are an old tradition in Bengal, but this time they are under attack. According to this Sabrang India commentary, on the night of 17 October a Kolkata Municipal Corporation squad arrived in Jadavpur with police and central forces to pull down a CPI(M) stall. The party says permission had been taken from the police, the corporation and the electricity department. Supporters held their ground all night and the squad went back, though the stalls of SUCI(C) and APDR were reportedly removed. The High Court gave interim relief, saying it would hear the party's petition on 20 October.

In Bangaon the matter swung between two benches of the court. On 15 October a single bench allowed the CPI(M) to set up a stall. The very next day, on the state's appeal, a division bench stayed this order. According to the article, the party filed at least ten complaints in Kolkata, five supporters were injured in Barasat, and in Malda the Bajrang Dal is accused of getting a stall shut. The BJP denies any role.

The article recalls that in September Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari reportedly said puja committees should not give space to stalls that write the word 'Sharadotsav' in place of Durga Puja. The writer argues that making space for a stall depend on its vocabulary or religious image is an ideological condition, not a neutral rule.

Article 19 gives the freedom of speech and of trade, with reasonable restrictions. The administration can regulate land, electricity and safety, but cannot use this as an excuse to suppress ideas. The article cites Germany in 1933, when after the Reichstag fire the opposition was pushed aside through emergency decrees and the 'Enabling Act', and makes clear that this is not equating Bengal with Nazi Germany but a warning.
nazar: A book stall attacks no one, it only offers an invitation to read. If selling Marxist literature in a festival crowd needs permission from a court, and a squad still arrives at night to tear it down, it shows how rattled power is by dissent.
The puja pandal has always been Bengal's shared public space. Dividing it on the terms of one ideology ends that very sharing.
sawal: Whose books may be kept in the festival's shared space?
ref: Sharadotsav
The autumn festival. A secular name used in Bengal for the Durga Puja season, which many Left and cultural groups adopt.
Enabling Act
A law passed by the German parliament in March 1933, which gave Hitler's government the power to make laws without the parliament's approval.

h: Pakistan: the same fault lines, the same results, again and again
dek: Maleeha Lodhi writes that hostility between government and opposition, centre-province clashes, a weak parliament and hollow institutions keep Pakistan going round in the same circle.
body: Maleeha Lodhi, who has been Pakistan's ambassador to the US, the UK and the United Nations, writes in Dawn that history in the country is repeating itself as tragedy and farce at the same time. Recent events have deepened the old fault lines that have been the root of instability for decades. In her view a powerful elite is holding the country in this very place.

The first fault line is between government and opposition. Between the Muslim League (Nawaz) government and the PTI, politics has become a war. Lodhi calls dishonest the claim by federal ministers linking the removed government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to terrorist groups. A culture of compromise never took root, and this is what opened the way for the army's interference. The 1973 Constitution, the 2006 Charter of Democracy and the 2010 Eighteenth Amendment were rare exceptions. According to Lodhi, the PTI became the largest party in 2024 yet was kept from forming the government, and its hard line today comes from this.

The second fault line is between the centre and the provinces. Just seven days after independence, the government of the North-West Frontier Province was dismissed, and every province has at some point suffered governor's rule. Lodhi also links this to the breakup of the country in 1971.

The third fault line is the helplessness of parliament. The 26th Constitutional Amendment of 2024 and the 27th of 2025 were passed without debate; members did not even get the draft beforehand. Both Houses also approved the emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa almost silently. The fourth fault line is the weakness of institutions, the biggest example of which is the judiciary, which according to the writer recent amendments have placed under the executive.
Lodhi believes these fault lines are not permanent, but bridging them needs bold leadership that breaks with the past.
nazar: Lodhi's list will feel familiar to an Indian reader too: laws passed without debate, the centre's friction with opposition-run governments, and questions over the independence of the courts. This story from next door shows that democracy survives not through elections but through the strength of institutions.
The heaviest burden of the emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa falls on its ordinary people, who are already being crushed between terror and military action.
sawal: When parliament becomes only a rubber stamp, where are the people to speak?
ref: Charter of Democracy
A 2006 agreement between Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif, in which both promised to oppose military interference and keep democratic norms.
Eighteenth Amendment
An amendment passed unanimously in 2010, which gave the provinces more powers and strengthened the parliamentary system.

h: Bangladesh needs reliable clean water, not new tube wells
dek: Ashraf Dewan and Mo Haque say the success of the 2.1 billion dollar plan should be measured by whether every home is still getting safe water ten years later.
body: The government of Bangladesh is in talks with partners such as UNICEF, the World Bank and WaterAid on a big drinking water plan of about 2.1 billion dollars, or 25,000 crore taka. Local Government Minister Abdul Moyeen Khan gave details of it on 8 October. The aim is to bring clean water to 18 crore people, at a time when rivers are drying up, water is being held back upstream and salinity is rising in the south.

Ashraf Dewan of Australia's Curtin University and Mo Haque, a hydrologist at Britain's University of Portsmouth, ask in The Daily Star whether five or ten years after this investment a family will still be able to drink clean water with confidence. In their view rural schemes have so far rested on counting: how many tube wells were installed, how many plants were built. But a tube well that breaks down, gets contaminated or is out of reach is not a water service.

The writers suggest that every village should have a minimum network of tested, working sources that everyone can reach. This should include government deep tube wells, repaired old wells, and also private tube wells whose owners agree to share water with neighbours. Before digging a new tube well, it should be checked whether an old well nearby can be fixed. The measure should not be the number of new tube wells but how many homes have a tested, working source.

They also talk of a digital system through which people can find out whether their water is contaminated with arsenic and where the nearest safe source is. The government department has such tools, but they are not linked with each other.

The most important suggestion is about accountability. According to the writers, the agency that supplies water should not be the only judge of its own work. An independent drinking water regulator should carry out surprise checks, look into failures and make the results public. Only then will clean water become a public service that keeps running.
nazar: This debate is just as important for India. The Jal Jeevan Mission has stressed counting tap connections, while in many villages the taps are dry or the water has arsenic and fluoride. The arsenic crisis of Bengal and Bihar is much like Bangladesh's.
As long as a count of infrastructure is taken to be a service, poor families will keep getting water on paper and keep drinking contaminated water in reality.
sawal: Is getting a tap the same as getting clean water?
ref: Arsenic pollution
A poisonous element found naturally in the groundwater of Bangladesh and eastern India, which raises the risk of skin disease and cancer.
DPHE
Bangladesh's Department of Public Health Engineering, which is responsible for drinking water and sanitation in rural areas.

h: What Trump's praise really holds for Pakistan
dek: According to former ambassador Touqir Hussain, US-Pakistan ties are better than in the Biden years, but it would be a mistake to see them as a deep strategic partnership.
body: In his column in Dawn, former ambassador Touqir Hussain asks what Donald Trump's repeated praise of Pakistan's leadership really means. His answer is that relations have certainly improved since the Biden years, but their standing has risen while their foundation has not changed.

According to the writer, this change has come less from any special importance of Pakistan and more from Trump's own whimsical, one-sided foreign policy. Amid his use of tariffs, his attitude towards China and Russia, and his lesser regard for old alliances, Pakistan happened to benefit.

There are concrete things too. A 68.6 crore dollar package for the maintenance and upgrade of Pakistan's F-16 fleet, a big radar assistance contract for 21 countries that includes Pakistan, growing economic cooperation in energy, IT, crypto, farming and critical minerals, and a counter-terrorism partnership. The US is also the biggest market for Pakistan's exports, and Washington has always had an interest in managing India-Pakistan conflict.

Still, the writer has doubts. In his view, behind Trump's rhetoric, policy is being shaped by traditional, China-focused officials who lean towards India, such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio. That neither Rubio nor any senior State Department official has visited Pakistan so far shows that talk of a strategic relationship is mostly just words. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling China the biggest economic and military threat shows the administration's real priority, and India policy flows from that.

The writer expects that Trump's personal-style policy may end with his term. But the damage done to America's standing by the US-Israeli wars in West Asia gives Washington a reason to stay engaged with Pakistan in future too. His conclusion is that this relationship is necessary, not indispensable, and Pakistan should keep it that way.
nazar: This column takes a needed note of caution about American closeness in South Asia. Taking a president's praise for policy has been an old mistake of smaller countries, and the writer rightly reminds us that Washington's real axis is China.
There is a lesson in it for India too. American ties rest on give and take, and keeping one's strategic freedom is in every neighbour's interest.
sawal: Will this warmth last after Trump?
ref: Strategic autonomy
The ability to set foreign policy according to one's own interest, without being tied to the camp of a big power.
A US-made fighter jet, which has been a key part of the Pakistani air force for decades and depends on American support.

h: More than 20 UN experts say: stop the crackdown on SIR protests
dek: The experts have called for an independent inquiry into the detention of more than seven thousand people in Delhi, the lathi charge on students and reports of sexual violence.
body: More than twenty independent UN human rights experts have told the Indian government that the crackdown on the ongoing protests against SIR must stop at once and that there must be a fair inquiry into police excesses. According to a Maktoob Media report, the experts called this action a violation of India's international obligations and said it is part of a larger and worrying pattern.

The experts' statement says that recently in New Delhi more than seven thousand people were detained and taken to detention centres set up far away. They included young people, journalists, human rights activists, lawyers and members of political parties. It is alleged that their phones were seized and all material related to the protest was deleted. Most of them, including the movement's leaders, were released after twenty-four hours.

According to the statement, the protests were peaceful, yet unarmed students were beaten with lathis (police batons) and thousands of people were stopped from reaching the protest. The experts expressed special concern over reports of sexual violence and gender-based abuse during the protests and in detention. They said they have warned the government several times before about restrictions on peaceful assembly, excessive use of force, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and the targeting of student activists.

The experts also questioned the use of Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, under which sweeping bans were placed on gatherings, public transport was stopped and the internet was shut down. Their demands are: excessive use of force must stop immediately, the blanket ban on gatherings must be lifted, the misuse of digital surveillance, including biometric surveillance, and of internet shutdowns must stop, and there must be an independent inquiry into the police and related forces so that victims get justice and compensation. They also asked for an assurance that this will not happen again.
nazar: When a government, instead of listening to its own citizens, packs them into buses, takes them far away and has the pictures deleted from their phones, questions on the international stage are bound to come. This statement shows that the question raised about the voter list has now become a question of civil liberty.
The government may brush this off as an internal matter, but it will also have to answer the allegations of sexual violence and the detention of seven thousand in the country's courts and Parliament.
sawal: Why is the government so afraid of peaceful protest?
ref: Section 163 of the BNSS
A provision that replaced Section 144 of the old CrPC, under which a magistrate can immediately ban gatherings and movement in an area.
UN Special Rapporteurs
Independent experts appointed by the Human Rights Council, who are not under any government and report on the state of rights in countries.

h: An order to block a page must be given to the user too: High Court
dek: The Punjab and Haryana High Court ordered a news company's Facebook page restored and said blocking it without giving reasons goes against natural justice.
body: The Punjab and Haryana High Court has said that if the government asks a social media platform to remove a user's page or content, a copy of that notice must also be given to the user at once. According to a LiveLaw report, Justice Tribhuvan Dahiya gave this ruling on a petition by Haryana 24 News Network Private Limited.

The company's Facebook page was blocked in India on 21 August 2026. This action followed a notice sent to Meta by the Superintendent of Police of Yamunanagar under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. The company said it got neither any prior notice nor a copy of the letter sent to Meta, so it did not even know why the page was shut. The state's position was that one of the company's directors is an accused in a criminal case and tried to intimidate the victim and witnesses through the page.

The court first found that under the 2021 IT Rules such a notice can only be sent by an authorised officer of at least DIG rank. An SP is below that rank, so the notice was outside his authority. The court also said that even if the rules do not clearly say the user must be told, natural justice requires that the user gets a copy. For this it cited the Supreme Court's 2023 MediaOne ruling.

The state had said the company should go to Meta's grievance system. The court rejected this argument, because when the user does not even know the reason for the blocking, how can they defend themselves. The court quashed the notice, directed that the page be restored within twenty-four hours, and said that if any notice is sent in future, the company must get a copy at once.
nazar: In recent weeks the accounts of journalists, cartoonists and protesters have been shut without reasons being given. This ruling puts on record a simple point: the one being silenced at least has the right to know why.
The real test will be whether governments and platforms follow this order in other cases too, or whether every user will have to run to court.
sawal: Under which law is it fair to silence a voice without giving a reason?
ref: Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act
On getting a notice from the government or its agency, a platform has to remove unlawful content, or else it may lose the legal protection it enjoys.
MediaOne ruling (2023)
While lifting the ban on the Malayalam channel MediaOne, the Supreme Court said sealed covers and decisions without reasons go against a fair hearing.

h: After a murder in Muzaffarpur, a mob burns six homes in a Dalit settlement
dek: After a young man was killed in the Karja police station area, an angry mob attacked a nearby Dalit settlement, and people ran for their lives.
body: In Bihar's Muzaffarpur district, after a young man was killed late on Saturday night, a mob stormed a nearby Dalit settlement and set fire to at least six homes. According to a report in The Mooknayak, twenty-year-old Navneet Kumar of Mohammadpur Khaje village in the Karja police station area had gone to a local fair with his friend Subhash Kumar, where he was attacked with a knife and died.

When the body reached the village after the post-mortem, people's anger flared up. It was said that one suspect in the murder is linked to the nearby Pratappur Dalit settlement. After this the mob attacked the settlement, beat people and burned at least six homes of Scheduled Caste families. The people of the settlement ran for their lives. There are also allegations of firing in the air to spread fear, which the police have not confirmed.

According to Ganesh Ram of Pratappur, Navneet had a quarrel with Gajendra Ram's son, whom he describes as linked to the illegal liquor trade. He alleges that a mob of more than fifty people attacked the settlement in a planned way. Fire engines arrived on news of the fire, but by then the homes had been badly burned.

Senior Superintendent of Police Kantesh Kumar Mishra, Rural SP Rajesh Singh Prabhakar and City SP Mohibullah Ansari reached the spot. According to the SSP, extra armed forces are deployed in the village, and the situation is tense but under control. He spoke of strict action against those who take the law into their own hands. A special team led by Saraiya SDPO Abhijeet Kaur is camped in the village.
nazar: One person was accused and the whole settlement was punished. In the caste structure this logic of collective punishment falls first on Dalits, whose homes are the flimsiest and whose voices are heard least.
The murder inquiry is one thing, but those who burned the homes must be booked at once under the SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act, and compensation must be paid for the burned homes.
sawal: Why was a whole settlement burned for one accused?
ref: SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
A law providing strict punishment for caste violence, humiliation and damage to property against Dalits and Adivasis, and relief for victims.
Collective punishment
Targeting a person's family, caste or whole neighbourhood for one person's alleged crime, which is completely forbidden in law.

h: Ajba Khatun returns home after 772 days in a detention camp
dek: The ailing woman from Barpeta who was declared a foreigner has been freed on conditional bail, but her case is still unfinished.
body: Ajba Khatun of Koetkuchi village in Assam's Barpeta district returned home on 13 October after being held for more than two years in the Matia transit camp in Goalpara. According to a report by Citizens for Justice and Peace (CJP) published on Sabrang India, she was declared a foreigner and detained on 2 September 2024. That day 28 Bengali-speaking Muslims of Barpeta were picked up.

The family was so poor that it could not even go to the High Court. CJP took up the matter, and in March 2025 the Gauhati High Court stayed her deportation and called for the Foreigners Tribunal's record. The main case remained pending and Ajba stayed in the camp. In September 2026, with two years completed and her health getting worse, the group stepped up efforts for her release on the basis of the Supreme Court's and the High Court's suo motu proceedings on detention during the Covid period.

Nanda Ghosh, in charge of CJP Assam, and Abhijit Chaudhary of the legal team filed an application through her son, found sureties and prepared the papers. On 11 October conditional bail was granted. On the day of release the team set out from Barpeta at dawn, brought Ajba from the camp, and the Border Police handed her over to the sureties. Under the condition she will have to report at Barpeta Sadar police station every week.

On the way Ajba described the camp as hell. She spoke of a blind woman named Sehra, whom she used to look after in the camp and who is still there. Sehra had pleaded with her that efforts be made for her release too. On reaching the village Ajba fainted several times. Her son works as a labourer in Meghalaya's coal mines and could not come. The report reminds us that the release is conditional and the legal fight remains.
nazar: An ailing, poor woman was kept locked up for more than two years while the High Court was considering her case. This shows how easily the citizenship check in Assam turns into punishment.
There is no public count of how many women like Sehra are in the camps with neither a lawyer nor a surety. While the case is pending, the very justification for detention is in question.
sawal: If the case is unfinished, what were the two years of imprisonment for?
ref: Foreigners Tribunal
Quasi-judicial bodies in Assam that decide whether a person is a foreigner or not, whose decisions have often been accused of bias.
Matia transit camp
The country's largest detention centre, built in Goalpara district, where people declared foreigners are held.

h: Manipur: three people out gathering wood are killed, bodies taken to the chief minister's house
dek: After firing by suspected militants on the border of Imphal East and Kangpokpi, angry people placed the bodies outside the chief minister's residence, and police fired tear gas.
body: In Manipur on Monday, protesters placed the bodies of two people killed in violence outside the house of Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh in Imphal. According to a Scroll report, these people were collecting firewood near the border of Imphal East and Kangpokpi districts when suspected militants opened fire on them. Imphal East has a larger Meitei population, while Kangpokpi is a Kuki-majority district.

Those killed were 35-year-old Arubam Ronil and 51-year-old Lairenlakpam Inaobi. Some others were injured in the firing. One of them, 32-year-old Kh. Sushil, later died, taking the death toll to three. A group had brought the bodies to Imphal to protest against the violence that has gone on since 2023.
An eyewitness told Scroll that police fired several tear gas shells to disperse the crowd. After this the bodies were taken to the Jawaharlal Nehru Institute of Medical Sciences.

The violence that broke out in May 2023 between the Meitei and Kuki-Zo-Hmar communities has still not stopped. After N. Biren Singh's resignation, the state was under President's Rule from February 2025 to February 2026. Kuki groups had alleged that Biren Singh's approach was biased. Khemchand Singh took over as chief minister on 4 February 2026.

In September the chief minister told the Assembly that at least 306 people have been killed since May 2023 and 49 are missing. About 60,000 people were made homeless, of whom 36,000 have been resettled and 24,000 are still in relief camps. Earlier this month there had been reports of nine people killed in twenty-four hours.
nazar: Even after three years, an everyday task like gathering wood in Manipur means risking one's life. In villages on the border between the two communities, ordinary people remain the easiest targets, and a change of government has not changed their safety.
Carrying bodies to the chief minister's door is a sign of despair. The answer should not be tear gas but a concrete political effort that restores trust.
sawal: Whose responsibility, in the end, is the safety of Manipur's border villages?
ref: Kangpokpi
A Kuki-majority hill district of Manipur next to the Imphal valley. Since the 2023 violence it has remained a key strip of tension between the valley and the hills.
President's Rule
Direct rule by the centre in place of the state government under Article 356. In Manipur it lasted from February 2025 to February 2026.

h: Two attacks in two nights on buses headed to Srinagar
dek: After Karnal in Haryana, stones were thrown at a Jammu and Kashmir-registered bus in Doraha in Punjab too, and Chief Minister Omar Abdullah spoke to the Haryana government.
body: Two incidents of attacks on buses going to Kashmir came to light on two nights in a row. According to a Siasat Daily report, at about eleven on the night of Sunday 18 October, stones were thrown at a bus headed to Srinagar in Doraha in Punjab's Ludhiana district. The bus driver, Ishfaq Ahmad, says some miscreants broke the bus windows while the passengers were asleep.

A night before this, a passenger bus headed to Srinagar was also pelted with stones in Karnal in Haryana. According to the police, the driver of this Jammu and Kashmir-registered bus and local people in a car had a quarrel over parking. It is alleged that two local men injured a passenger and broke the bus windows with bricks. A dhaba (roadside eatery) worker was also injured.

The driver, Waqar, said people at the dhaba stopped him from parking and said a Jammu and Kashmir vehicle would not stop there. On a written complaint by the dhaba owner, police detained two people. DSP Rajeev Kumar gave the media details of the incident.

Nasir Khuehami, who has kept raising the issues of Kashmiri students, wrote on social media that the Doraha incident was the second attack in a day and that an elderly Kashmiri passenger was injured in Karnal. Chief Minister Omar Abdullah said his office had spoken to the Haryana government and had been assured of strict action under the law.
According to the report, there is no information on any arrest in the Punjab incident, nor has any statement come from the police or the state government.
nazar: Stopping a vehicle or throwing stones at it after seeing its number plate shows how common suspicion and hatred towards Kashmiris have become. If a Kashmiri traveller passing through the rest of the country is not safe even on the highway, the talk of 'one nation' sounds hollow.
It is easy to brush such incidents off as parking disputes. The Punjab and Haryana governments should send a clear message that discrimination against the people of any region is a crime.
sawal: Since when did a Jammu and Kashmir number plate become a reason for suspicion?
ref: Doraha
A town in Punjab's Ludhiana district on the Delhi-Amritsar national highway. Buses from Delhi to Jammu and Kashmir pass through here.

h: A week into a hunger strike, Jamia forms a committee
dek: To talk with students on hunger strike since 12 October for the restoration of the students' union, the administration has set up a seven-member high-level committee.
body: As students' indefinite hunger strike at Jamia Millia Islamia completed a week, the university administration on Monday 19 October set up a high-level committee of seven members. According to Siasat Daily, this step is an attempt to ease the tension created by a clash between students and security staff and the detentions that followed.

The committee includes the vice-chancellor, Registrar Prof. Mohammad Mahtab Alam Rizvi, deans of various faculties, the Dean of Students' Welfare, the Chief Proctor and the hostel provost. Meanwhile MP John Brittas wrote to Vice-Chancellor Prof. Mazhar Asif, appealing to him to resolve the differences.

The students have been on hunger strike since 12 October and their main demand is the restoration of an elected students' union. The administration had dissolved the students' union, citing violence and disorder on campus. Ebin Basil, a student on hunger strike, says student representation has now shrunk to departmental elections only, whose councils are headed by deans or heads of department, so students are left with no role in decisions.

According to the students, the administration gave no answer on questions such as the fee hike, the lack of basic facilities, alleged irregularities in admissions and the reservation policy. It is alleged that security guards beat Jasim Khan, a student on hunger strike, and that Delhi Police later detained him.
The administration has expelled Ebin Basil, while Jasim Khan and Rehan Haider have been suspended. The report does not say when the committee will meet or whether the students have accepted it.
nazar: A committee for talks on one side, and the expulsion and suspension of hunger-striking students on the other: this double approach does not build trust. There is not a single elected student representative on the committee, while the very root of the dispute is that students' voices have been shut out of decisions.
Turning dissent in a university into a matter of discipline weakens the foundation of democratic education. Without the punishments being withdrawn, the talks will remain incomplete.
sawal: How will a committee formed without students hear the students?
ref: Students' union
A body elected by students in a university that puts their demands before the administration. In many central universities its elections have been put off for years.
Rustication
The punishment of removing a student from an institution for a set period or for good, the harshest form of disciplinary action.

h: Even after the monsoon, reservoirs 31 percent empty, and the South in crisis
dek: According to the Central Water Commission's latest data, storage in the country's 178 big reservoirs is about a quarter lower than last year, with the Cauvery and Pennar basins worst off.
body: Even after the monsoon has left, the country's big reservoirs have not filled up. Citing the Central Water Commission's weekly bulletin of 15 October, a Down To Earth report says the 178 big reservoirs monitored by the commission hold 126.7 billion cubic metres of water, which is 68.58 percent of their total live capacity. In other words, about 31 percent is empty.

This storage is 24.5 percent lower than at the same time last year and 16.4 percent below the average of the past ten years. These 178 reservoirs hold about 72 percent of the country's total live reservoir capacity, so their state gives a picture of the whole country.

The biggest worry is in the South and West. In the Cauvery basin storage is 60 percent below normal, and in the Pennar 72 percent. The Krishna, Sabarmati, Mahi and Kutch-Saurashtra basins are also short. Reservoirs such as Tamil Nadu's Mettur, Andhra Pradesh's Somasila and Srisailam, Kerala's Idukki, Karnataka's Tungabhadra and Ghataprabha, and Maharashtra's Jayakwadi, Ujani and Manjara are below even half their normal level.

On the other hand, storage in the Narmada, Mahanadi and Subarnarekha basins is above normal, while the Ganga, Godavari, Tapi and Brahmaputra basins are close to normal. Of the 20 reservoirs linked to hydropower, 12 are at or below normal.

The report warns that this may hit irrigation, drinking water and power generation, all three. This year the monsoon was about 12 percent below average in the country and 24 percent below in the South, and drought-like conditions are building up in several states.
nazar: If reservoirs are half empty in October itself, the crisis up to summer is already in sight. Farmers sowing the rabi (winter) crop, poor city neighbourhoods that depend on tankers, and workers migrating because of drought will be the first to bear the blow.

Shortages in basins like the Cauvery and Krishna can also flare up old water disputes between states. Governments should from now on put drinking water and the needs of small farmers first in sharing water.
sawal: Who gets the water of half-empty dams first?
ref: Central Water Commission
A technical body under the Ministry of Water Resources that every Thursday issues a bulletin on water storage in the country's big reservoirs.
Basin
The whole area that gets water from a river and its tributaries. The state of reservoirs is often assessed basin by basin.

h: An accident on the farm, then the government's indifference: disabled farmers hit twice
dek: The stories of farmers from Yavatmal and Solapur show how an injury or illness from farming turns into debt and loneliness, and the state does not even keep count of them.
body: Ravindra Shinde, 47, of Umri village in Yavatmal district farms 16 acres. In October 2021, amid strong winds and rain, he climbed a pole to save his harvested soybean and restore power to the motor pump. He got an electric shock and his left arm had to be cut off at the shoulder. Now he has to hire labourers for every task, so his costs are about one and a half times those of other farmers, while the 2,500 rupees a month he gets from the government does not cover expenses.

Nilesh Wankhede, 27, a Dalit farmer from Injala village in the same district, fainted at 19 while spraying pesticide on cotton. His eyesight never fully came back, and working long in the sun is not possible. His ageing parents now look after the two-and-a-half-acre farm. Nilesh does not have a UDID disability card; his eyes have not even been tested.

Suresh Mundhe of Ukadgaon in Solapur has lived with polio since childhood. In the 2025 floods his 15,000 chickens drowned. Going by the government rule he should have got 15 lakh rupees, but because of a limit of 100 chickens he got only 10,000 rupees. The limit has now been relaxed, but the paperwork remains, and Mundhe has a debt of 40 lakh.

The report points to the lack of data. In Maharashtra more than 36 lakh people are entitled to a UDID card, but only about 14 lakh cards have been made. The state has neither a separate count of disabled farmers nor any special scheme for them.

Parth M.N. explains that the weather now turns suddenly and demands quick decisions, which disabled farmers often cannot take. Crops sell below the support price and fertiliser has also become costlier after the Iran war, which means every new blow falls harder on a farmer already carrying a burden.
nazar: Farming is not even counted among the country's most dangerous jobs, so an injury on the farm comes under neither insurance nor policy. How will a state that does not even know the number of its disabled farmers make a scheme for them?

Rules like the compensation limit show that the relief system was never built with small and vulnerable farmers in mind. UDID cards will have to be made by holding camps village by village, and farm accidents will have to be recorded as a separate category.
sawal: Whose responsibility is a farmer disabled on the farm?
ref: UDID card
An identity card from the central government for persons with disabilities, needed to get pensions and the benefits of welfare schemes.
Vidarbha
The eastern region of Maharashtra, which includes districts such as Yavatmal, Amravati and Nagpur and has been known for farmer suicides for two decades.

h: Palamu: sixty years of irrigation schemes, and fields still wait on the sky
dek: In Jharkhand's Palamu, lift irrigation, dobhas, wells and canals were all built, but with no upkeep farming still depends on the rain.
body: The land that Kaushal Kishore Vishwakarma, 52, of Darudih village in Palamu looks at once had crops swaying in it; now there is only grass. Twenty years ago a lift irrigation scheme brought water to the village from a river a kilometre and a half away, and even a summer crop was possible in ten villages. The scheme ran for about five years, then a pipe broke and was never fixed. Now he sows paddy only in the rains in the low-lying fields, and nothing in the rabi (winter) season.

Jharkhand has declared drought ten times in about the last 25 years. In the back-to-back droughts of 2023 and 2024, almost everyone from Darudih left in search of work. The district's soil conservation officer accepts that big money was put into lift schemes, but there was no upkeep and middlemen ate up the money.

In 2015-16 about 2,500 dobhas, or small farm ponds, were built, but they have not been audited in ten years and no one knows how many remain. In Chianki village the canal of the Mandal Dam project lies dry. According to Basant Singh, farming there has been halved and every fourth man works as a labourer outside.

In the 1966 famine, wells, ponds and check dams were built in the name of relief. Shrikrishna Oraon, 72, of Budhibir village says an ahar from that time still makes paddy farming possible in his area. Even so, about 92 percent of Jharkhand's farming depends on rain, and less than five percent of land in Palamu is irrigated.

This year, from 1 June to 4 August, Palamu got 48 percent less rain than normal, and by 21 July paddy sowing had not reached even one percent of the target, while by the same date last year it had reached 107 percent. The department advises short-duration varieties, but Basant Singh does not know a single farmer who got free seed.
nazar: The story of Palamu shows that in the fight against drought what is lacking is not money but upkeep and accountability. There is interest in building schemes and cutting ribbons, but there is no budget or anyone responsible for joining a broken pipe.

When fields dry up, villages empty out and workers end up in Bengaluru or Surat. A social audit of irrigation works and giving the gram sabha (village assembly) the right to look after them: this is the concrete way to stop migration.
sawal: Why does it take twenty years to fix a broken pipe?
ref: Lift irrigation
A system that lifts water from a river or reservoir by pump and carries it to fields on higher ground, where water cannot flow on its own.
Ahar-pyne
The traditional irrigation system of south Bihar and Jharkhand, in which rainwater is held in an ahar (pond) and carried to fields through pynes (channels).

h: Thailand: Karen indigenous people taken from their ancestral forest and sent to Myanmar
dek: 26 people from Ban Pa Deng, a Karen village in Kaeng Krachan National Park, were sent across the border for lacking citizenship papers.
body: On 10 August 2026, in Thailand's Phetchaburi province, district and forest officials along with the army raided Ban Pa Deng, a Karen indigenous village inside Kaeng Krachan National Park. The targets were people who could not prove Thai citizenship. 28 people were caught, including eight children and two pregnant women. According to Human Rights Watch, two were released after their records were checked, and the remaining 26 were sent to an immigration detention centre in Bangkok.

On 19 August these 26 people were sent towards Myanmar from a border checkpoint in Kanchanaburi, where the Karen National Union's Fourth Brigade received them. The community's worry is about ten people who had been removed earlier and handed over to the Myanmar army and an armed group linked to it. There is no contact with them now.

Human rights groups argued that such deportation violates Thailand's obligations under the UN Convention against Torture, because in Myanmar these people face the risk of violence or forced military recruitment. It is also not clear whether their citizenship claims were checked before they were removed. The families say they have lived in this very forest for generations.

The Karen community had lived in these forests long before the park was created. Since then they have been uprooted again and again and resettled on land where their traditional farming is not possible. In 2021 UN experts, citing forced evictions, the burning of a village and the killing of community leader Porlajee Rakchongcharoen, had appealed for World Heritage status to be put off, but the status was granted.

According to the writer, the matter looks like one of papers but is really about land. Conservation rules take away access to ancestral land, this weakens both livelihoods and documents, and then the lack of documents itself becomes the excuse for eviction.
nazar: This story is not unknown to India. Both patterns run here too: removing Adivasis from tiger reserves and national parks, and calling people 'infiltrators' by demanding citizenship papers.
If conservation makes the forest's real guardians homeless and stateless, it protects not nature but power. Tools like the Forest Rights Act were made to break exactly this cycle.
sawal: Who removes the people of the forest in the name of saving the forest?
ref: Kaeng Krachan
Thailand's largest national park, which borders Myanmar and was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.
Karen National Union
The political organisation of Myanmar's Karen people, whose armed wing has been fighting the Myanmar army for decades.

h: Floods in a Bihar short of rain, and relief only on paper
dek: Despite 35 percent less rain, about 50 lakh people in 15 districts of Bihar are hit by floods, but help has not reached the villages of Katihar.
body: In Gandhi Tola in Manihari, Katihar district, waist-deep water fills the three-room mud house of 35-year-old Geeta Devi. Her husband works as a daily labourer in Delhi, so she looks after the house, the fields, the cattle and four children. The government says 1,260 community kitchens and 13 relief camps are running, but Geeta's family has got nothing. She borrowed 1,500 rupees for bamboo and tarpaulin.

According to the state government's statement of 14 September, about 50 lakh people in 15 districts are affected. The Ganga, Kosi, Burhi Gandak, Punpun, Bagmati and Ghaghara are above the danger mark at many places. The strange thing is that Bihar got 35 percent less rain than normal this monsoon. According to water expert Dinesh Kumar Mishra, this time the flood did not come from Nepal but from heavy rain in UP and Bihar in the last phase of the monsoon.

Himanshu Thakkar lists several reasons behind this: land that was first dry and then suddenly soaked, shrinking forests and disappearing ponds, and the water backing up from the Farakka Barrage, which slows drainage and increases silt.

Pradeep Kumar Mandal, former sarpanch (village head) of Hanswar village, says about a thousand acres of crops are under water in his panchayat and camps have been set up only in towns. The sons of 65-year-old labourer Sudesh Mahto have already gone away in search of work. The government has not yet released figures for the loss of crops, cattle and homes. Eklavya Prasad of the Megh Pyne Abhiyan says their 2024 survey found the average loss per family to be about five and a half lakh rupees.

In neighbouring Jharkhand's Sahebganj too, about 45,000 families are affected. Farmer Pintu Yadav's three acres of fodder were washed away. The report concludes that the water will recede, but debt, broken homes and migration will stay for a long time.
nazar: Bihar's floods are now not just nature's blow but also a failure of policy. When the figures of loss are not even recorded, compensation too comes arbitrarily and late, and the hardest blow falls on women whose husbands work as labourers far away.
Without an honest debate on barrages, embankments and shrinking forests, the same story will return every year. Relief camps should be near the flooded villages, not in towns.
sawal: When there was less rain, why did villages go under?
ref: Farakka Barrage
A barrage built on the Ganga in West Bengal in 1975, which has long been blamed for silt build-up and worsening floods in Bihar.
Megh Pyne Abhiyan
A social campaign working on water, sanitation and disaster-related issues in the flood-hit areas of Bihar.

h: Shoot the People: a photographer who writes movements with his camera
dek: This Al Jazeera Witness film follows British-Nigerian photographer Misan Harriman's camera to grassroots activists around the world who are out on the streets for equality and civil rights.
body: The film 'Shoot the People', released on 8 October in Al Jazeera's documentary series Witness, is woven around the work of British-Nigerian photographer and activist Misan Harriman. The film is directed by Andy Mundy-Castle. The title itself is a play on words: in English 'shoot' means both to fire a gun and to take a picture. The film sets the second meaning against the first, that is, recording people instead of taking aim at them.

According to Al Jazeera, Harriman is a visual storyteller who first became known for his pictures of the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests. That year, after George Floyd's death in police custody in the US, protests against racism and police violence spread beyond America to many cities around the world, including London. Harriman's pictures from that time travelled very far on social media and brought him wide recognition as a photographer.

The film's introduction says that the second big part of his work is linked to the Palestinian protests. After the Israeli attacks on Gaza there were big marches again and again in London and European cities, and Harriman's camera was present at these processions too. The film sees these two movements not as separate events but as parts of one long fight for equality and justice.

Harriman is also known in the world of fashion and famous faces. He became the first Black man to shoot a British Vogue cover, and he has photographed celebrities such as Angelina Jolie, Lewis Hamilton, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. The film rests on this contrast: the same camera that works in glittering studios also records the faces of ordinary people on the street with equal respect.

The real centre of the film, in Al Jazeera's words, is the grassroots activists around the world who keep struggling for equality, civil rights and social justice. Harriman's pictures become a way of bringing out these people's grit and patience. The film wants to show that it is not lone heroes but collective action that is the real force making any society more just.

The strength of the Witness series has been that it pauses on the human beings behind big news. Around this week the same series has carried films on families scattered across Gaza and across borders. 'Shoot the People', unlike them, looks towards the people who raise their voice against such conditions, and towards the photographer who turns their voice into pictures.
nazar: The picture of a protest often shrinks to crowds, police and clashes. The value of a photographer like Harriman is that he gives the protester a face, a name and dignity, which makes it hard for power to simply call them a 'troublemaker'.

In India too, from the farmers' movement to Shaheen Bagh, pictures have shaped the memory of movements. The question is who will do this work of recording when those holding cameras are themselves targets.
sawal: Can a picture change the direction of a movement?
ref: Black Lives Matter
A movement that began in the US against police violence and racism towards Black people. After George Floyd's death in 2020 it spread around the world.
Witness
Al Jazeera English's documentary series, in which independent filmmakers make films on the lives and struggles of ordinary people.

h: The man after getting a job: six poems by Nishant
dek: Nishant's new series of poems on Sammukh looks at the relationships, home and mind that change on the journey from unemployment to a job.
body: On 20 October Sammukh published six poems by the poet Nishant, tied together by a single thread: the job. Nishant teaches at Kazi Nazrul University in Asansol and has received the Bharatbhushan Agrawal Award and the Devishankar Awasthi Samman. According to the editorial note, this series is the next stage of his earlier poem that recorded the struggle of an unemployed young man. Now the same young man has got a job, and the poems feel their way through the change within him. Some of them have been published before, some are new.

The first poem is about the joy of getting a job at thirty-four, but there is a sting in that joy too. The family is full of pride, while the poet remembers the debates of university days, full of talk about revolution and society, which have now dissolved into everyday worries. The second poem goes through the reverse situation: a younger friend he once guided has come back with a job, and an unspoken distance has come between the two.

The third and fifth poems are the sharpest part of the series. In them the job looks like a new class divide, almost a new caste system, which separates the secure from the insecure. In one poem the relationship between two people gets stuck not on caste or qualities but on the status of a small contractual government job.

The other poems go inside the home. In one, an elder brother who depends on the younger one's earnings takes out his bitterness on him, and the poem records this tension in a conversational tone. The last poem is in the voice of a sister who, while holding the family together, watches her youth pass in instalments, like a long train journey. To read the poems in full, see the Sammukh link.
nazar: This series is the story of a generation for whom a job is no longer a livelihood but a certificate of social identity. Where contracts and temporary posts have become common, a permanent job creates a new high and low, which seeps even into relationships, marriage and friendship.
Nishant's strength is that he does not make the one who gets the job a hero. Alongside the joy, the question of what was lost stays present in the poems throughout.
sawal: Has the job become the new caste of our times?
ref: Devishankar Awasthi Samman
A prestigious award for Hindi criticism, started in memory of the young critic Devishankar Awasthi.
Bharatbhushan Agrawal Award
A well-known award given every year to young Hindi poets for a single poem.
