h: The living who copy the dead: Calvino's invisible cities, in Hindi
dek: The fourteenth instalment of Suman Shekhar's translation has cities like Eusapia and Beersheba, where the places of life and death, of the real and the copy, are turned around.
by: Italo Calvino, translated by Suman Shekhar
body: A Hindi translation of the Italian writer Italo Calvino's book 'Invisible Cities' is being published in instalments on Sammukh. This translation by young fiction writer Suman Shekhar began in July, and its fourteenth instalment came out on 20 October. In the book Marco Polo tells Kublai Khan about cities that are on no map, and each city is a form of human desire, memory or fear.

The first city in this instalment is Eusapia, beneath which lies its twin city. Its people dry their dead and take them below, where instead of work and trade they live in life's happy moments: feasts, dances, music. Slowly it emerges that the dead below make some changes every year and the living above begin to copy them. In the end it becomes hard to say which city is the real one.

The second city is Beersheba, whose people believe there is a heavenly Beersheba of gold and silver in the sky and a hell of filth beneath the ground. So they hoard precious things and avoid small joys. Here Calvino turns the whole picture over: this obsession with perfection is in fact the closed, mechanical city below, and the true sky is made of the things the city throws away without a thought.

At the start of the instalment there is also a passage on cities by the Canadian poet Anne Carson, and the editorial note sees it as another form of Calvino's imagined cities. The language of the translation is easy, and the full text can be read on Sammukh.
nazar: Calvino's cities fit today's India strangely well, where copying maps made up from the past is being turned into the agenda of the present, and everyday life is being put off in the name of a promised 'heaven'.
Good translations of world literature are still few in Hindi. A web magazine patiently bringing a whole book to readers instalment by instalment is valuable work in itself.
sawal: Which dead dreams are we living in imitation of?
ref: Italo Calvino
A twentieth-century Italian fiction writer (1923-1985), whose 'Invisible Cities' came out in 1972 and is seen as a model of imaginative prose.
Anne Carson
A Canadian poet, translator and classical scholar who writes by mixing poetry, essay and Greek literature.

h: Naxalbari, a play and the mystery of the Chinese diplomats
dek: Using government files, journalist Shantanu Nandan Sharma's book Rebel Bastar asks how big China's role was in the 1967 Naxalbari uprising.
body: Senior journalist Shantanu Nandan Sharma's English book Rebel Bastar: History, Maoism and the Search for Answers in India's Heartland came out from Hachette India in July. This report by the Bhasha news agency, published on ThePrint Hindi, focuses on the chapter of the book that examines the Naxalbari uprising and China's alleged role in it.

The story begins on 23 May 1967. A few hours before the peasant uprising broke out in north Bengal, two Chinese diplomats arrived in Calcutta as special guests to watch Utpal Dutt's Bengali play Ajeya Vietnam (Invincible Vietnam). The play was against American military action in Vietnam, and the then foreign minister M.C. Chagla had told Parliament that it contained insulting remarks about Indira Gandhi and the government.

In Parliament the opposition asked whether the Chinese officials had reached Calcutta just before the violence. Chagla's answer was measured: they had gone to Calcutta, not Naxalbari, and they may have given support from there. The report makes clear that this does not prove China set up the uprising.

In July 1967 China's People's Daily published an editorial praising Naxalbari and suggested to Indian revolutionaries the Maoist path of building bases in villages and encircling the cities. Citing documents of the Ministry of External Affairs and Parliament, Sharma says that the draft of a Lok Sabha answer made sharp allegations against China, but that language was removed from the final answer that went out in Indira Gandhi's name.

According to the writer, these changes show the dilemma after the 1962 war: there was worry about Chinese interference, and also the compulsion not to raise tension with Beijing. The book's larger argument is that Maoism in Bastar did not arrive suddenly; it is a new form of a centuries-old tradition of Adivasi resistance against power, and of the administration's failure.
nazar: Calling Naxalbari a foreign conspiracy has always been easy for those in power, because it pushes the questions of land, sharecropping and hunger into the background. The documents themselves accept that no proof of Chinese instructions was found.
The same mistake is being repeated in Bastar today. Until the question of the Adivasis' forests, minerals and rights is settled, guns and operations will not bring peace.
sawal: Whose convenience is it to look for the roots of a revolt outside?
ref: Naxalbari uprising
An armed uprising of landless peasants in Naxalbari in Darjeeling district in May 1967. The Naxalite movement got its name from it.
Utpal Dutt
A major actor-director of Bengali theatre and cinema, known for his political plays, who also went to jail.

h: A decade of time, society and literature in Kaushal Kishore's book
dek: At the National Book Fair in Lucknow, Jan Sanskriti Manch held a discussion on Kaushal Kishore's book of criticism 'Samay, Samaj aur Sahitya', which the speakers called a record of the past decade.
body: According to a report in Samkaleen Janmat, on 5 October, on the literary stage of the National Book Fair in Lucknow, Jan Sanskriti Manch released and discussed poet and critic Kaushal Kishore's book 'Samay, Samaj aur Sahitya' (Time, Society and Literature). The session was chaired by senior writer and translator Shakeel Siddiqui. He said the past decade, which saw the pandemic and the movements against the citizenship law, was a time of extraordinary upheaval, and this book directly confronts that very time.

Opening the discussion, poet and fiction writer Dr. Shailesh Pandit called the book a written account of historical consciousness, which measures the path from the days of Premchand and Nehru to today. According to him, the book connects Indian literature with the Naxalbari movement and with writers of resistance such as Nagarjun, Pash, Varavara Rao, Saroj Dutta, Cherabanda Raju and Sri Sri, and farmers, labourers, women and mine and factory workers are at its centre.

Critic Dr. Usha Rai said the book has 29 essays, which touch almost every form, such as poetry, fiction, essay, reportage, drama, autobiography, translation and criticism. In her view the first essay, on Naxalbari, casts its shadow over the whole book. She saw in it an inner voice in the tradition of Kabir, and made special mention of the essay on Virendra Yadav's criticism and of a review called 'Modinama'.

Kumar Vinitabh, national secretary of the Janvadi Lekhak Sangh, underlined the book's ideological commitment, its link with people's struggles and its scientific outlook. Dinesh Priyaman, a writer from Unnao, remembered the late critic Virendra Yadav and said that like him, Kaushal Kishore's eye too is more on the people at the margins than on the 'nation', and the book is ideologically firm but not rigid.

Prof. Ramesh Dixit, who could not come because of illness, sent a written message calling it a good collection of critical reviews. The session was conducted by Farzana Mahdi, secretary of JASAM Lucknow, and at the end the writer spoke about how the book came to be made.
nazar: Through one book, this report recalls a tradition of criticism that does not read literature apart from the movements of its time. Threading everything from Naxalbari to the movement against the citizenship law into one string is part of this outlook.
In the report all the speakers speak in almost one voice, so no debate on the book's weaknesses is seen. The publisher's name is also not in the report.
sawal: Should criticism be a record of its own time?
ref: Jan Sanskriti Manch
A Left-leaning organisation of writers and cultural workers, formed in 1985, which speaks of linking literature with people's movements.
Naxalbari movement
A peasant uprising that began in 1967 in Naxalbari village in Bengal, which deeply influenced literature in many languages, including Hindi.
